books.title: Pre-Salvation
books.description: This book explains the human condition apart from Christ, God’s kindness and witness, why people cannot save themselves, and how believers can care for those who do not yet know Jesus.

lessons.title: Dead in Trespasses and Sins

scripture.text: And you He made alive, who were dead in trespasses and sins.

lessons.explanation: Paul describes people apart from Christ as spiritually dead because of sin. He is not saying they are physically dead or unable to show kindness. He means that sin has broken humanity’s relationship with God and that people cannot create spiritual life for themselves.
lessons.matters: Ephesians 2 continues with the good news: God is rich in mercy and makes people alive with Christ. Salvation begins with God’s grace, not human achievement. This diagnosis should produce humility and gratitude, not contempt for people who do not yet believe.
remember: This teaching should be understood alongside the whole Bible passage, not as an isolated slogan.
Do not use this truth to look down on others; respond with humility, love, and dependence on God.

lessons.title: Separated from God by Sin

scripture.text: But your iniquities have separated you from your God; and your sins have hidden His face from you.

lessons.explanation: Sin is more than breaking a rule; it damages our relationship with the God who made us. Isaiah describes sin as separating people from God. The problem includes real guilt and real distance from God.
lessons.matters: The gospel answers both sides of the problem. Through Jesus, sin is dealt with and people are brought back into peace and fellowship with God. We should therefore speak about salvation as forgiveness and restored relationship.

lessons.title: Under the Wrath and Judgment of God

scripture.text: He who does not believe is condemned already… and he who does not believe the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God abides on him.

lessons.matters: This truth should make the gospel urgent, but it must never make Christians cruel or self-righteous. We share the warning with humility, remembering that salvation is offered through God’s love in Christ.

lessons.title: Common Grace: God’s Kindness to All

scripture.text: For He makes His sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust.

lessons.explanation: Common grace is God’s kindness to people generally, including those who do not yet believe. Life, food, relationships, beauty, abilities, social order, and many good gifts are examples of His kindness.

lessons.title: The Insufficiency of Good Works

scripture.text: For by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, lest anyone should boast.

lessons.explanation: Good actions matter, and the Bible calls believers to do what is good. But good works cannot erase past sin or purchase God’s acceptance. We cannot turn salvation into a wage that God owes us.
lessons.matters: Ephesians 2:8–10 holds the ideas together: salvation is God’s gift received through faith, not earned by works; then those who are saved are created in Christ for good works. Good works are the result of salvation, not its price.

lessons.title: The Bondage of the Will to Sin

scripture.text: Most assuredly, I say to you, whoever commits sin is a slave of sin.

lessons.explanation: Sin is not only a list of wrong actions; it can become a power that enslaves our desires and choices. Jesus said that the one who practises sin is a slave to sin. People may make real choices, but sin distorts what they love and how they use their freedom.
lessons.matters: Jesus offers freedom from sin’s mastery. This does not mean believers never struggle again. It means Christ begins a new life in which sin is no longer their rightful master, and they learn to live in obedience through His help.

lessons.title: Religion Without Regeneration

scripture.text: This people honors Me with their lips, but their heart is far from Me.

lessons.title: Seeing People as God Sees Them

scripture.text: But when He saw the multitudes, He was moved with compassion for them, because they were weary and scattered, like sheep having no shepherd.

lessons.explanation: Jesus looked at people with compassion. He saw more than their outward behaviour or social position; He saw people who were weary, vulnerable, and in need of God’s care. Christians are called to see people as persons made in God’s image and worthy of dignity.
lessons.matters: Compassion is not approving every action or ignoring truth. It means speaking truth with patience, listening carefully, serving where possible, and desiring another person’s good. Gospel concern should lead to loving action rather than criticism.

lessons.title: Fully God, Fully Man

scripture.text: And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.

lessons.explanation: The Bible teaches that Jesus is truly God and truly human. He did not stop being God when He became human; the eternal Son took on a real human nature. He experienced human life, including hunger, tiredness, sorrow, and suffering.
lessons.matters: Because Jesus is God, He reveals God and has power to save. Because He is truly human, He can represent us and sympathise with our weakness. Christians should avoid imagining Jesus as partly God or merely a good human teacher.

lessons.title: His Substitutionary Death

scripture.text: He Himself bore our sins in His own body on the tree.

TEACHER AND FACILITATOR GUIDE How to teach each lesson • Start by asking learners what they already know about the subject. Do not assume prior theological knowledge. • Read the Bible passage aloud and explain its setting before explaining individual phrases. • Teach the definition first. Then explain the idea in short steps and give a familiar example. • Pause to check understanding. Invite learners to explain the main point in their own words. • Use reflection questions for honest thought, not to shame or pressure learners to disclose private matters. • Use the comprehensive check to identify what needs reteaching. Correct misunderstandings gently and return to the Bible passage. • End with a practical response that is realistic and connected to the lesson. Suggested assessment approach A learner has understood a lesson when they can (1) define its main idea, (2) explain the Bible passage in context, (3) distinguish the teaching from a common misunderstanding, and (4) describe a practical response. For open-ended questions, assess clarity and biblical understanding rather than requiring identical wording. Important editorial note This simplified edition preserves the curriculum’s module and lesson titles and supplies a clear teaching framework for every lesson. Some Christian traditions interpret particular subjects—especially baptism, assurance, and aspects of end-times teaching—differently. Teachers should explain their church’s position fairly, distinguish clear biblical statements from areas of disagreement, and encourage learners to read Scripture in context.
